## Welcome

I am a PhD candidate in Applied Economics at Oregon State University on the
2026–27 economics job market.

My research examines interactions between private land use and natural disaster risk, and how privately rational decisions
can generate large-scale social costs and benefits. I use causal inference
methods, spatial datasets, and natural resource economic theory to understand how
disaster risk drives landowner adaptation. I then ask how this adaptation can
change future risk, generate externalities, and create a role for public policy.
My work contributes to the climate change adaptation literature, as well as the
rapidly growing wildfire literature in economics and the natural sciences.

My job market paper examines how changing wildfire risk in the western United
States has affected private forest management decisions, providing the first
empirical test of long-standing economic theory. Linking confidential plot-level
forest inventory data with wildfire perimeters and fire-season weather, I find
that more wildfire activity and warmer, drier weather shocks lead landowners to
harvest earlier and plant at lower densities. A bioeconomic Monte Carlo
simulation shows that this adaptation has reduced forest volumes by 7–10% since
2000. However, adaptation also changed the amount of fuel on the landscape. In
the 2020 wildfire season, landowner adaptation caused \$63–72 million in damages
from increased wildfire PM2.5, but produced \$28–58 million in climate benefits
from lower CO2 emissions. Overall, adaptation produced net social damages, but a
policy requiring landowners to reduce fuels after harvest could create net
social benefits.

**Job market paper:** [Landowner Expectations of Wildfire Risk Have Accelerated
Harvest, Reduced Volume, and Altered Fuel Loads in Western U.S.
Forests](research.qmd) &nbsp;[PDF](papers/jmp.pdf){.btn .btn-outline-primary .btn-sm} [Slides](papers/jmp-slides.pdf){.btn .btn-outline-primary .btn-sm}
